description: I’m a high school student passionate about space, robotics, technology, and programming. I bring creativity, problem-solving, research, and teamwork. I’m looking for motivated teammates skilled in coding, game development, UI/UX, design, or space science to build an amazing mission game!
summary:
Project Ore-Bitting is a browser-based space mission game for ages 8–13. Players plan and fly a complete mission to any or all the planets of the solar system and even the moons. In Mission Control, they pick a destination (a planet or moon) and route, choose how much fuel to carry, and select 4 of 9 gadgets. Fuel takes up space, so more range means fewer gadgets. After launch, the player gets shown a cutscene of the rocket ship flying to the selected planet. On arrival, players switch to either the deployed rover’s or drone’s view depending on the type of planet or moon in order to collect samples. Each sample is added to a Pokédex-style index of 22 real materials (Ore-Dex), such as tholins, helium-3, and methane ice. 
The game addresses the challenge by turning mission trade-offs (fuel, mass, supplies, instruments) into choices with visible consequences. A tool that works on Mars may be useless on Titan, so the game teaches why the right instrument unlocks the right discovery. It runs as a HTML5 game with real planetary data, making space engineering accessible to young students.
details:
Project Ore-Bitting has two phases. In Mission Control, the player clicks a planet or moon in a 3D solar system and sees info about it, with hover explanations for hard terms. They choose a route, set how much fuel to carry, and pick 4 of 9 gadgets. Fuel tanks take up space, so more range means fewer gadgets.

After the player confirms the plan, a cutscene shows the rocket flying to the chosen world. On arrival, the game switches to a rover’s or drone’s view, depending on the terrain (a gas giant, for example, needs a drone). The player picks a gadget and uses it on a glowing sample site to collect a sample. The wrong tool gives a plain reason why it won’t work. Each sample is added to a Pokédex-style index of 22 real materials (Ore-Dex), such as tholins, helium-3, and methane ice. Undiscovered materials appear as silhouettes, and hovering over one shows which worlds it’s found on.

Benefits

  • Fuel, mass, and instruments trade off against each other, so every choice has a visible consequence.
  • Players learn why a tool suits a terrain, not just that it does. A drill that works on Mars may be useless on Titan.
  • Hover explanations and a collection goal make it approachable for beginners.
  • There is no single perfect loadout. What a player discovers depends on what they chose to bring.

Intended impact

We want young students to understand that space missions come down to planning and trade-offs, not just rockets. We also want them curious about the materials that make up other worlds. The game is free and runs in a browser, with nothing to install. As well as to build passion in the kids for astronomical studies.

Tools and technology

  • HTML5, CSS, and JavaScript (ES modules)
  • Three.js for the 3D solar system, cutscene, and surface scenes
  • Local JSON data files for planets, materials, and gadgets, based on real planetary data
  • Hosted on itch.io as a HTML5 game
  • Claude Code for a lot of the code, including scene setup, audio, menus, and the gadget and material systems.
  • Manual coding by our team to debug, fix, and tune what the SI produced, and to add features, mechanics, and polish.

Creativity

  • Players plan a real mission and then see it through, from choosing fuel to examining a sample.
  • Fuel takes up gadget space, so players trade range against capability.
  • Gadgets are based on real NASA hardware, such as JPL’s LEMUR climber, the EELS snake robot, and cryobot ice-melters.
  • The Oré-Dex gives a young player a reason to visit every world, including the moons.
  • Rovers and drones suit different terrains, which gives each destination its own challenge.

Factors we considered

  • Audience: ages 8–13, so the science is simplified but kept accurate.
  • Accuracy: real planet data, real mission-based gadgets, and the real material-to-world matches.
  • Accessibility: no installation, plain-language explanations, and hover definitions.
  • Scope: a short hackathon timeline, so we cut the in-flight failure system and focused on planning and sample collection.
  • Balance: fuel and gadget limits are tuned so no single loadout is clearly best.
